transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
President Trump held a state dinner last night for Chinese President Xi Jinping after a day of talks,
and PR's Jennifer Pak reports from Beijing.
According to an official Chinese readout, President Xi told Trump the two sides should work on AI guardrails
and keep the technology under human control.
He says he hopes the U.S. will oppose Taiwan independence and treat Chinese companies fairly in the U.S.
because the two sides had an agreement in May. But the U.S. has continued to sanction more Chinese firms
over national security concerns.
Xi says he and Trump maintain deep and close communication as the two sides continue to hammer out a better deal.
Jennifer Pak, NPR News, Beijing.
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted more missiles fired at it by Yemen's Houthi rebels.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has launched more airstrikes in missiles across parts of Yemen.
And PR's Aya Betrawi reports.
Saudi Arabia's military says six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis were intercepted on Thursday.
The Iran-backed Houthis have been targeting Saudi Arabia with drones and missiles.
Last week, they hit a Saudi airbase in Taf and have hit Aramco energy facilities.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has been carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen.
It comes as the Houthis routed Saudi-backed fighters from key territory in Yemen, overlooking the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has launched more than a thousand airstrikes and missiles at Yemen in past weeks.
The United Nations Human Rights Office says 32 civilians, among them 15 children,
have been killed in airstrikes and shelling in Yemen since the start of August.
And more than 125,000 people have been displaced.
Aya Betrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
A new TV ad is out featuring President Trump. It's paid for by the U.S. government.
It shows several images of Trump while featuring words that say, quote, "largest tax cut in history."
The music repeats the phrase, quote, "love me."
New Hampshire Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan is seeking answers, saying the ad appears to violate federal law.
The state of New York is suing the prediction market site Poly Market.
NPR's Bobby Allen reports the suit alleges the platform is an illegal gambling operation.
New York officials are asking a judge to push Poly Market out of the state.
Prediction markets have exploded in popularity in Trump's second term,
taking in billions of dollars in weekly bets on everything from elections to war
to the word choice of politicians and sports announcers.
More than two dozen lawsuits have been filed against the sector, which, in addition to Poly Market, includes its rival, Kalshi.
Legal watchers say a case will likely eventually make its way to the Supreme Court.
In a statement, Poly Market said it will fight for its users.
The company insists it is not a gambling operator, but a company that offers a financial product known as an events contract,
something overseen by the Trump administration.
Donald Trump Jr. is a Poly Market advisor and investor.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
Poly Market is countersued.
This is NPR.
The Pentagon says it's looking for several missing parts from an F-35 fighter jet.
Australia says it was returning the parts to the U.S. for repair, but the shipment was diverted to Hong Kong.
Then it disappeared.
The U.S. says China is engaged in extensive espionage to find out more about advanced U.S. weapons.
Harmful disease outbreaks spread by wildlife are on the rise worldwide.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports on new research showing humans are driving many outbreaks, but in complicated ways.
Humans can influence risk for diseases in lots of ways.
Cutting down the rainforest might bring people into closer contact with harmful animal viruses or climate change could be pushing disease-carrying mosquitoes to new places.
But figuring out just how much influence humans have is tricky.
A new study in the journal Nature tried to answer that question by creating a big global map.
Researchers pinpointed over 50,000 instances of someone getting diseases like Ebola, impacts or dengue.
Then they analyzed how human activity, including deforestation and climate change, influenced risk.
Humans influenced virtually all of these diseases, though no one factor drove them all.
But access to health clinics boosted the likelihood of detecting an outbreak.
The authors say investing in health care can keep an outbreak from spreading.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
Thousands of people turned out in a sports stadium yesterday in Pretoria, South Africa, trying to set a record.
They're trying to break the world record for the biggest cookout.
Organizers say they were aiming for 3,000 people for the big grill.
The Guinness Book of World Records has not yet determined if they set the cookout record.
This is NPR.
